title: The Verity Piecers
description: A quilt guild in Marchfield: meeting minutes, the block of the month with the cutting written out, the comfort quilt count, the raffle quilt, and one obituary.

data.author: Ellen Vraber
data.tagline: Second Thursday, 6:30, the community room. Bring a machine or do not.
data.about:
The Verity Piecers, a quilt guild, founded 1987 in the basement of the Marchfield library by nine people, six of whom are still on the roll.

Regular meetings the second Thursday of the month at 6:30 p.m. in the community room at the Marchfield Public Library, 114 Ward Street. July is the picnic. December is the party and the auction. Dues are $25 a year as of February 2026. Fifty-eight on the roll.

Hand quilting group meets Tuesdays nine to two at the Nye Mills Grange hall, in the frame, all year. Anybody may sit down at it.

[b]Comfort quilts to date: 971[/b], counted since 2009. County General, the Kerrin ambulance, [url=synth://ashkettlevfd.org/]Ashkettle Station 4[/url], the county foster care office and the St. Mark's pantry.

This website is written by Ellen Vraber, secretary, who also writes the minutes, and who is not a web person and has said so. Comments are read. Most of them are not from people.

posts.title: Minutes, April 10, 2025
posts.body:
Verity Piecers, regular meeting, Thursday 10 April 2025, community room, Marchfield Public Library. Called to order 6:34 p.m. by Peg Sarnow. Thirty-one members present, two guests.

Minutes of 13 March approved as posted.

[b]Treasurer's report[/b] (Amsler). Balance 6 March, $1,318.44. In: dues $140, raffle tickets $86. Out: batting order $211.60, postage $16.79, hosting $27 for three months. Balance 3 April, $1,289.05. Filed for audit.

[b]Comfort quilts[/b] (Feeney). Nine out since the last meeting. Six to County General, three to the Kerrin ambulance. Running total since we started counting in 2009 is 792. Marge has fourteen tops waiting on backs and has now asked twice.

[b]Program.[/b] Deb Strick brought four samples off her longarm and talked about backings for forty minutes. The part she said three times: three and a half inches of extra backing on all four sides, and press it. She will not load a backing that has not been pressed. She says this pleasantly and she means it.

[b]Show and tell.[/b] Nita Kohlman, Storm at Sea, 68 by 84, edge to edge in a feather. Jeanne Ostrowski, two placemats and an apology for the placemats. Arla Wendt, a nine patch in shirtings, hand quilted, nine to the inch, which she said was slow going now. Bev Oakerson, a t-shirt quilt for her nephew, every block fused to a light knit interfacing, which she recommends and which about half the room does not.

[b]Old business.[/b] July meeting is the picnic at the Bradgate shelter again. Motion by Kohlman to keep the date and the shelter, second by Feeney, carried 29-0.

[b]New business.[/b] Dues. Carol Yaggi raised the question of going from $20 to $25 to cover the hall insurance rider. Discussion. No motion made. It will come back and everyone knows it will come back.

Adjourned 8:21 p.m. Next meeting 8 May.

Respectfully submitted, E. Vraber, secretary.

posts.title: Block of the month for 2026: the plan and what to buy
posts.body:
Posted for Nita Kohlman, who wrote all of this and does not want a login.

Twelve blocks, one a month, all of them 12 inches finished and 12 and a half unfinished. They are all traditional and none of them is hard. If your block does not come out at 12 and a half, the block is not wrong, your quarter inch is.

[b]Buy this now, before January, and buy it all at once.[/b]

[list][*]Background: 4 yards of one light. One. Do not start with a bleached white and finish with a natural because the shop ran out. You will see it in the finished quilt from across a room and so will a judge.[*]Darks and mediums: scraps, or twelve fat quarters if you want twelve blocks that match each other. A fat quarter is 18 by 22 and every block below fits inside one.[*]Sashing: 1 and 3/4 yards.[*]Cornerstones: a fat eighth.[*]Border: 1 and 1/4 yards, cut crossgrain.[*]Binding: 1/2 yard, which is seven strips at 2 and 1/4 inches.[*]Backing: 4 and 1/4 yards, two lengths seamed across the width, selvedges trimmed off before you seam them.[/list]

[b]The setting.[/b] Three blocks across, four down. Sashing 2 inches finished, cut 2 and 1/2 by 12 and 1/2, thirty-one pieces. Cornerstones 2 and 1/2 inches cut, twenty of them. That gives a centre of 44 by 58. Border 4 inches finished, cut 4 and 1/2 wide: two at 58 and 1/2 for the sides, two at 52 and 1/2 for the top and bottom, pieced where they have to be and pressed toward the border.

Finished quilt 52 by 66. Backing wants to be 60 by 74 so Deb has her three and a half inches all the way round.

[b]Thread.[/b] 50 weight 3-ply cotton, one colour, grey or beige, for the whole year. Change your needle after about eight hours of sewing. An 80/12 sharp is right for quilt cotton and a universal is not wrong, it is just not as good.

Blocks are posted here the week after each meeting with the cutting written out. Nobody has to keep up. Arla did four blocks of the 2019 sampler and finished the top in 2022 and it was fine.

comments.author: Sue Ann Ficke
comments.body: First year doing one of these. Is 4 yards of background really right, that seems like a lot.

comments.author: Nita Kohlman
comments.body: It is right and you will have some left. Twelve 12 inch blocks eat about 2 and 1/2 yards of background between the squares and the triangles, and the extra is there because somebody every year cuts a 5 and 1/4 square when it says 5 and 7/8 and needs to cut it again. That somebody is usually me.

comments.author: Arla Wendt
comments.body: Buy it all at once. In 2013 I ran out of the background in August and the shop in Halsey had the same bolt number and it was not the same white.

posts.title: Minutes, January 8, 2026
posts.body:
Verity Piecers, regular meeting, Thursday 8 January 2026, community room, Marchfield Public Library. Called to order 6:33 p.m. by Peg Sarnow. Twenty-six present. Karen unlocked the room at six and we are on the lights and the thermostat, which is the same arrangement as last year and the year before.

Minutes of 11 December approved as posted.

[b]Treasurer's report[/b] (Amsler). Balance 4 December, $1,441.90. In: dues $200, December raffle $54. Out: hosting $27, domain renewal $18, ribbon order for the show $96.40. Balance 2 January, $1,554.50.

[b]Comfort quilts[/b] (Feeney). Eleven out in December. Running total since 2009, [b]861[/b]. Twenty-nine of those went to the foster care office at the county building, which is the most we have sent there in one year, and the number of placements that office reported for the year is in Ruth Cannady's write-up: [url=synth://thequarry.news/]thequarry.news[/url]. Marge sizes the totes off that number and has done since 2021.

[b]Program.[/b] None. January is the sort-and-price night for the show. Seven boxes of donated fabric were sorted, three were priced, and two boxes went back in the closet because they are polyester and nobody will say so to the woman who brought them.

[b]Old business.[/b] Dues. Motion by Yaggi to raise annual dues from $20 to $25 effective 1 February 2026, second by Oakerson. Discussion, eleven minutes. Carried 22-4. Roll is 58. Paid so far, 41.

[b]New business.[/b] Block of the month starts this month, see the November post. Nita has the cutting sheets printed and there are twenty-two of them and she is not printing more.

Bev reported the raffle quilt top is pieced and goes in the frame at the Grange hall the first Tuesday in February.

Adjourned 8:06 p.m. Next meeting 12 February.

Respectfully submitted, E. Vraber, secretary.

posts.title: Block one: Ohio Star
posts.body:
Posted for Nita Kohlman. Twelve inches finished, 12 and a half unfinished, nine units at 4 inches finished.

[b]Cut, per block[/b]

[list][*]Background: four 4 and 1/2 inch squares (corners), two 5 and 1/4 inch squares (for the star points)[*]Dark: one 4 and 1/2 inch square (centre), two 5 and 1/4 inch squares[/list]

[b]Quarter square triangle units, four of them, 4 and 1/2 unfinished[/b]

Pair one background 5 and 1/4 square with one dark 5 and 1/4 square, right sides together. Draw once corner to corner on the back of the light. Sew a scant quarter inch either side of the line. Cut on the line. You have two half square triangles. Press to the dark. Do the same with the second pair.

Now put two of those half square triangle units right sides together with the light on the dark, seams nested and opposing, and draw a line on the back perpendicular to the seam. Sew a scant quarter either side, cut on the line, press. That is two quarter square units. The second pair gives you the other two.

Square them to 4 and 1/2 with the diagonal of your ruler on the diagonal seam and the 2 and 1/4 mark on the centre. The centre is where the four points meet and it should sit a quarter inch down from the top raw edge. If it does not, your scant quarter is not scant.

[b]Assemble[/b]

Three rows of three. Corner, point unit, corner. Point unit, centre, point unit. Corner, point unit, corner. Press the rows in opposite directions, nest, sew, press the two long seams open or to one side, it does not matter here and it will matter in March.

[b]Why it is first[/b]

Because everything else this year is half square triangles, quarter square triangles or squares, and this block is all three of them in one place. If you get 12 and a half out of this you will get 12 and a half out of the rest.

Bring it on 12 February. Nita is not grading them.

comments.author: Sue Ann Ficke
comments.body: Mine came out 12 and 3/8. Four times in a row, same amount each time.

comments.author: Nita Kohlman
comments.body: Then it is the seam and not you. Sew two 2 and 1/2 strips together, press, measure the finished width. If it is 4 and 3/8 instead of 4 and 1/2 you are taking a sixteenth too much on every seam and there are eight seams across that block. Move the needle one position right or put a piece of blue tape on the bed and sew to the tape.

comments.author: Sue Ann Ficke
comments.body: 4 and 3/8. Tape it is. Thank you.

comments.author: Marilyn Hesch
comments.body: I have been quilting since 1991 and I have never once squared a quarter square unit and I am not starting now.

comments.author: Nita Kohlman
comments.body: Marilyn's quilts are fine. Marilyn also presses with steam from four inches away like she is annoyed at it. There is more than one way.

posts.title: Block two: Bear's Paw
posts.body:
Posted for Nita Kohlman. This one finishes at 14 inches, not 12. It is the only odd one this year and it gets its own row at the bottom with a 12 inch strip beside it. Nita says she has been planning this since 2024 and Peg says that is not an excuse, and both of those things are true.

Seven by seven grid of 2 inch units.

[b]Cut, per block[/b]

[list][*]Dark: four 4 and 1/2 inch squares (the pads), sixteen 2 and 7/8 inch squares (for the claws)[*]Background: sixteen 2 and 7/8 inch squares, four 2 and 1/2 inch squares (the outer corners), four 2 and 1/2 by 6 and 1/2 rectangles (the sashing)[*]Accent: one 2 and 1/2 inch square (the centre)[/list]

[b]Claws[/b]

Thirty-two half square triangles at 2 and 1/2 unfinished, two inches finished. Pair each dark 2 and 7/8 with a background 2 and 7/8, draw, sew a scant quarter either side of the line, cut, press to the dark, trim the dog ears. Sixteen pairs gives thirty-two units. Eight units to a paw.

[b]One paw, 6 and 1/2 unfinished[/b]

Row one: two claws with the dark pointing up and away from the pad, then a background 2 and 1/2 square on the outside corner. Row two, going down the side: two claws with the dark pointing out, then the 4 and 1/2 pad. Sew the two claws in row one into a pair, add the corner square, sew that strip to the top of the pad. Sew the side pair, add nothing, sew it to the side of the pad. The pad is 4 and 1/2, the side strip is 2 and 1/2 by 4 and 1/2, the top strip is 2 and 1/2 by 6 and 1/2.

Make four. Two of them are mirrored and two are not, and the way to tell is that every claw points away from the centre of the block. Lay all four on the table before you sew any of them to the sashing. Everybody in this guild has sewn a paw on backwards including the woman writing this.

[b]Assemble[/b]

Paw, sashing, paw. Sashing, centre square, sashing. Paw, sashing, paw. Six and a half plus two and a half plus six and a half is fifteen and a half raw, fourteen and a half unfinished after the two seams, fourteen finished.

[b]Note[/b]

The 2 and 7/8 squares are the ones people cut at 2 and 1/2 because 2 and 1/2 is the number they have been cutting all week. Read the line twice. Sixteen of one and sixteen of the other, and they are not the same.

comments.author: Bev Oakerson
comments.body: Cut thirty-two at 2 and 1/2. All of them. Did not notice until I had sewn four.

comments.author: Nita Kohlman
comments.body: I wrote the note about that in the post and you still did it, which is why I wrote it.

comments.author: Bev Oakerson
comments.body: I read the post after.

comments.author: Reva Detwiler
comments.body: For anyone hand quilting this one later: do not press those claw seams open. Thirty-two units of open seam in a 14 inch block and you will be putting a needle through a single thread of cotton all afternoon. To the dark and live with the bulk.

posts.title: Our January block is on a website that is selling it
posts.body:
Three people have now sent me the same link, so here it is in one place and then I am done with it.

The January block post is on a site that sells quilt patterns as PDFs at $6.99 each. The text is ours with the contractions taken out and the word "simply" put in eleven times. The photograph is Nita's block on Nita's kitchen table, and you can see the corner of the placemat Jeanne apologised for at the April meeting. It is being sold as [i]Vintage Country Star Quilt Block Pattern - Instant Download[/i]. The site is [url=synth://quiltpatternvault.shop/]quiltpatternvault.shop[/url] and it does not load for me either.

I looked into what we could do about it for about an hour, which is fifty minutes longer than it deserved. There is no address on the site and no name. The contact form does not submit.

So, plainly, because people are cross on our behalf and that is kind but I would rather they were not.

You cannot steal an Ohio Star. It is older than the state and it was never ours. Nita did not invent it and neither did the woman who taught her. What they took is a photograph of somebody's kitchen table, and the fix for that is that the photographs here are now 900 pixels wide and I am not putting anyone's table in one again.

If you want to be useful about it, buy a pattern from a shop that has a person in it. There are two left within driving distance and one of them is [url=synth://bobbinandbolt.synth/]Bobbin and Bolt[/url] in Bowes City, which is fifty-one miles, and the other is not answering its phone.

comments.author: mod_dcarver
comments.body: Nothing to do and nowhere to send it. I get about forty of these a morning on the boards and the answer is the same: delete it, do not argue with it, it is not a person. Nine hundred pixels is the right call.

comments.author: Lissa Vollmer
comments.body: Same thing happened to a binding photo of mine in 2024 off the county instance. It came back with a watermark on it that was not mine, selling a book that does not exist.

comments.author: Marilyn Hesch
comments.body: Pennyrile in Halsey is the one not answering the phone. It is not the phone. Sharon closed on the 6th. There is a sign.

comments.author: Ellen Vraber
comments.body: I did not know. I will take it off the blogroll at the weekend and I am going to leave it up there until then.

posts.title: Minutes, March 12, 2026
posts.body:
Verity Piecers, regular meeting, Thursday 12 March 2026, community room, Marchfield Public Library. Called to order 6:31 p.m. by Peg Sarnow. Thirty-four present, which is the most since 2023, and it is because the raffle quilt was on the wall.

Minutes of 12 February approved with one correction: the February hosting figure was $9, not $19.

[b]Treasurer's report[/b] (Amsler). Balance 5 February, $1,612.85. In: dues $325, raffle tickets $214, fabric sale at the sort night $88. Out: hosting $9, batting, two rolls of 80/20 at $121 each, $242, ticket printing $34. Balance 5 March, $1,954.85.

[b]Comfort quilts[/b] (Feeney). Nine out since February. Running total since 2009, [b]884[/b]. Four to County General, five to the foster care office. The hospital has asked us again to stop putting a pocket on them. There is one member still putting a pocket on them.

[b]Raffle quilt[/b] (Oakerson). Top is in the frame at the Nye Mills Grange hall. Tuesdays, nine to two, anyone may come and quilt and anyone may come and not quilt. Arla Wendt is doing the centre feathered star herself and expects to be at it into May. Row 2 of 9 at the meeting.

[b]Program.[/b] Carol Yaggi on entering the home arts department at the fair. The entry book comes out in June, entries close the Friday before, and the premium in the pieced classes is $8 for a first and $5 for a second and has been $8 and $5 since 2011. Carol's point, which she made twice: the class only exists if somebody enters it.

[b]Show and tell.[/b] Eleven blocks from February, all Bear's Paw, two of them with a paw on backwards and both owners knew and showed them anyway.

[b]Old business.[/b] Show date confirmed, Saturday 3 October, 4-H building at the fairgrounds, 9 to 4. Motion by Feeney to set the entry fee at $3 a quilt with a limit of three quilts per member, second by Hesch, carried 31-0.

[b]New business.[/b] Sue Ann Ficke asked whether the guild would buy a second design wall. Discussion. The guild's design wall is flannel stapled to four sheets of foam board and cost $31 in 2016. Motion by Ficke to build a second one, second by Yaggi, carried. Budget $40.

Adjourned 8:44 p.m. Next meeting 9 April.

Respectfully submitted, E. Vraber, secretary.

posts.title: The raffle quilt, and where the money goes
posts.body:
[img:photo:raffle-quilt-2026-frame]

[b]Feathered Star, 82 by 82.[/b] Centre star 24 inches finished, set on point, which makes the centre 34 square once the setting triangles are on. Those were cut oversize and trimmed back, because a feathered star squared up after the fact hangs better than one eased in.

Out from there: a plain frame at 4, a flying geese round at 6, a plain frame at 5, a sawtooth at 3 and a plain outer at 6. Thirty-four and twice twenty-four is eighty-two. Binding 2 and 1/4 inch double fold, straight of grain, joined on the bias.

Pieced in February at two sew-ins by Bev Oakerson, Nita Kohlman, Marilyn Hesch, Jeanne Ostrowski, Reva Detwiler and Sue Ann Ficke, who had been in the guild six weeks and got handed the sawtooth border.

Hand quilted in the frame at the Nye Mills Grange hall, Tuesdays, nine to two. Arla Wendt is doing the centre star, all of it, alone, at nine to ten stitches an inch. The rest of us are on the background at whatever we get, which in my case is six.

Fabric is quilt shop cotton throughout. Batting is an 80/20 off the roll we bought in February, which quilts to a maximum of 4 inches apart and is nowhere near 4 inches apart on this one. Backing is a single wide muslin, so no seam.

[b]Tickets[/b] are $1 each or six for $5. Two thousand printed. Any member may take a book. Turn in the stubs and the money to Dot, together, in the envelope, and write your name on the envelope. Every year somebody turns in money with no stubs and we cannot put those tickets in the drum.

Drawn at the show, Saturday 3 October, at 3:30 p.m. You do not have to be present.

[b]Where the money goes.[/b] The batting fund. That is it. It is a line in Dot Amsler's book, not a foundation, and it has no board and no website. Two rolls of 80/20 cost us $242 in February and made twenty-six comfort quilts. Last year's raffle brought in $1,340 and bought eleven rolls across the year.

posts.title: What a comfort quilt has to be
posts.body:
Posted for Marge Feeney. Print this and put it in the box with your fabric. It changes about once every four years and it has just changed.

[b]Sizes[/b]

[list][*]County General, adult: 50 by 60. Not bigger. It has to sit on a person in a chair without touching the floor.[*]County General, isolette: 24 by 30.[*]Kerrin ambulance and Ashkettle Station 4: 36 by 48. These go in a tote on the truck and they are given away at the scene and never come back, which is the point of them.[*]Foster care office: 60 by 80, twin. A child who is moved once is usually moved again, and the quilt should fit the next bed.[/list]

[b]The isolette ones have their own rules and they are not negotiable[/b]

100 percent cotton top, back and thread. Cotton or 80/20 batting, nothing else. No minky, no fleece, no flannel backing. Quilted closed at 3 inches maximum, not tied, no ties anywhere. Nothing sewn on: no buttons, no beads, no ribbon, no rickrack, no eyes. No batiks, because of the wax residue, and yes, it is washed out, and the answer is still no because the answer comes from the hospital and not from me.

[b]Everything else[/b]

Prewash what you use if you like, or do not, but do not mix a prewashed fabric with a fabric that has not been. Binding machine stitched down front and back. Not hand stitched. These go through a 140 degree wash and a commercial dryer and a hand stitched binding will not last a year, and a comfort quilt that is falling apart is worse than no quilt.

Label: printed cotton, sewn on, no names on it. Just "Verity Piecers" and the year. The hospital asked for no names in 2014 and gave us a good reason and I am not going to repeat the reason here.

[b]Where we are[/b]

Twenty-two out in the last six weeks, which is the most in any six weeks since 2019 and is almost entirely the March sew-in. Running total since 2009 is [b]906[/b].

Fourteen tops waiting on backs. It is always fourteen. I do not understand it either.

comments.author: Marilyn Hesch
comments.body: Has anyone told the church groups about the buttons. I saw two quilts in the foyer at Christmas with buttons on.

comments.author: Marge Feeney
comments.body: They are not ours and they are not going to the hospital. They are going to the pantry and a button is fine at the pantry.

posts.title: Minutes, May 14, 2026
posts.body:
Verity Piecers, regular meeting, Thursday 14 May 2026, community room, Marchfield Public Library. Called to order 6:35 p.m. by Peg Sarnow. Twenty-eight present.

Minutes of 9 April approved as posted.

[b]Treasurer's report[/b] (Amsler). Balance 2 April, $2,088.10. In: dues $75, raffle tickets $386, show entry fees $9. Out: hosting $9, show insurance rider $145, design wall materials $38.60. Balance 7 May, $2,365.50. Raffle receipts to date $600 on 717 tickets.

[b]Comfort quilts[/b] (Feeney). Eleven out. Running total since 2009, [b]917[/b]. Still fourteen tops waiting on backs.

[b]Raffle quilt[/b] (Oakerson). Row 6 of 9. Arla finished the centre star on 5 May and it is off the frame rollers and pinned to the guild's design wall at the Grange hall so people can see it. Bev counted the feathers. There are 144.

[b]Program.[/b] Machine clinic. Deb Strick and Reva Detwiler. Nine machines on the tables. Six of the nine problems were the machine being threaded with the presser foot down. One was a bent needle. One was a bobbin case in backwards. One was a 1952 Featherweight with a seized motor that Deb took home and which is not a clinic problem, it is a project.

[b]Show and tell.[/b] Fifteen blocks. Three people have all four blocks done. Two people have none and both said so cheerfully.

[b]Old business.[/b] Show, 3 October. Sign-up sheet for the hanging crew went round and has six names, and we need ten. Hanging starts Friday 2 October at 4 p.m. and is finished when it is finished.

[b]New business.[/b] The August meeting falls on 13 August, which is the Thursday of the fair and the draft horse show. Motion by Yaggi to cancel the August meeting, second by Hesch, carried 26-1. The August sew-in moves to Saturday 22 August at the Grange hall.

Adjourned 8:29 p.m. Next meeting 11 June.

Respectfully submitted, E. Vraber, secretary.

comments.author: Sue Ann Ficke

comments.author: Deb Strick
comments.body: The Featherweight is a 221, serial says November 1952. The motor is not seized, the grease in the gearbox has gone to varnish. It wants stripping and a wick. Give me six weeks and it will go to whoever in the guild will use it rather than put it on a shelf.

comments.author: Arla Wendt
comments.body: 144 is right. I counted them in February and I was not going to say so and spoil it for Bev.

posts.title: Minutes, June 11, 2026
posts.body:
Verity Piecers, regular meeting, Thursday 11 June 2026, community room, Marchfield Public Library. Called to order 6:32 p.m. by Peg Sarnow. Thirty-one present.

A minute was kept for Arla Wendt of Milbrook, a member since 1994, who died at home on Saturday 6 June. The secretary was asked to write something for the website and will.

Minutes of 14 May approved as posted.

[b]Treasurer's report[/b] (Amsler). Balance 7 May, $2,365.50. In: dues $50, raffle tickets $302, memorial gifts to the batting fund $240. Out: hosting $9, one roll 80/20 $121. Balance 4 June, $2,827.50.

posts.title: Arla Wendt, 1936-2026
posts.body:
Arla Wendt died at home in Milbrook on Saturday 6 June. She was eighty-nine. She joined this guild in 1994 and she was in the hand quilting group from the week it started.

Arla quilted two hundred and ninety-six quilts for other people and wrote every one of them down. The notebook is a spiral one from the drugstore on Ash Street, the kind with the wire that catches on everything, and each line has a date, a name, a size, and what she was paid, and nothing else, not one adjective in thirty years of it. She charged a cent and a half a square inch from 1996 and never raised it, and when Deb Strick told her in 2019 what a longarm gets for an edge to edge she wrote the number in the margin, looked at it a while, and did not raise it then either. The last line is 9 March 2026, a double for a woman in Coyne Flats, eighty-four by ninety-six, and beside it $120.96, because she worked it out every time and she never rounded it. She finished that one in five weeks with the frame pulled across to the window, the ceiling fixture in that room not having worked since Carl died. She quilted nine to ten stitches to the inch. She would have told you eight.

Carl Wendt died in 2011. They sold the herd in 1991 and she started taking in quilting the next winter, because the milk cheque had been the thing that paid the fuel bill and then it was not there. She used a hoop until 1998 and after that a frame Carl built out of two-by-fours and four C-clamps, which stands at the Grange hall and which her daughter Kathy has given to the guild. A size 11 between. Glazed cotton thread, one strand, never a knot on the back. A silver thimble with the top worn clean through that she would not replace, and would not discuss.

She marked with a chalk wheel run along a yardstick because she could not draw a straight line freehand, and she said so every time she did it, for thirty years, in the same words. She was wrong about prewashing and knew she was wrong and went on being wrong. If you started that argument she would let you finish it and then thread her needle.

She is survived by her daughter, Kathy Ruddy of Tessler, four grandchildren, and a sister, Lorene Hupp of Nye Mills. She was preceded in death by her husband and by a brother, Emil Ludeke.

Calling hours are Thursday 18 June from 4 to 7 p.m. at [url=synth://ostranderfh.synth/]Ostrander Funeral Home[/url] in Tessler. The service is Friday at 10 at Zion Lutheran in Milbrook. She asked for no flowers. Memorial gifts go to the guild's batting fund, which is a line in Dot Amsler's book and not a foundation, and which buys 80/20 by the roll.

She did the centre of this year's raffle quilt, the feathered star, all of it, by herself, between February and 5 May. Reva Detwiler and Jeanne Ostrowski are finishing the rest of it. It will hang at the show on 3 October and it will be drawn there and the money will go where it always goes.

Milbrook has not had a paper of its own since October 2016. So it goes here.

posts.title: The Ledger ran one too
posts.body:
Four people sent it to me, so here it is once.

[url=synth://now.verityledger.com/]The Ledger's current site[/url] published an obituary for Arla on 21 June under the byline Ledger Newsdesk. Nobody from this guild was asked for anything and nobody at that address answers a telephone, which I know because I tried the number on the page and it is a fax line at a Pinelock office in another state.

What it says, and what is actually so.

[list][*]"Arla Wendt-Ludeke." Her name was Arla Wendt. Ludeke was her name before 1957 and she did not hyphenate it and neither did anyone else.[*]"Age 91." She was 89. Born 14 November 1936.[*]"Of Marchfield." Milbrook. She lived in the same house on Bethel Road for fifty-four years.[*]"A lifelong member of the Verity County Quilting Society, founded in 1974." There is no Verity County Quilting Society. We are the Verity Piecers and we were founded in 1987 in the basement of the Marchfield library by nine people, six of whom are still on the roll.[*]"She is survived by her husband, Carl." Carl died in 2011. The paper that is now that site ran his obituary.[*]"The group has donated more than 3,000 quilts to local charities." 933 at the June meeting. We have counted every one of them since 2009 and the count is in the minutes on this website every month.[/list]

The photograph is not of Arla and it is not of her work. It is the guild's 2016 raffle quilt, a Lone Star, photographed on the steps of the 4-H building by whoever took pictures for the [url=synth://milbrookgazette.com/]Milbrook Gazette[/url] that year. The Gazette stopped in October 2016. Its site is still up. The picture is still on it. That is presumably where this came from.

I sent a correction through the form on the page. It returned a reference number and a message saying a member of the editorial team would review my submission within five business days. That was nine days ago.

I am writing this down here because this is the part of the internet where it can be written down. If you want the account of her that a person wrote, it is [url=/post/arla-wendt]two posts back[/url].

posts.title: Twelve to Station 4
posts.body:
Marge Feeney and I took twelve lap quilts out to the Ashkettle volunteer fire department on Wednesday. Station 4, on Route 62. Thirty-six by forty-eight, machine quilted, machine bound, cotton, no pockets.

They go in a grey tote on the tanker. If a house goes at two in the morning the people who come out of it are standing in a yard in whatever they had on, and somebody hands them one, and that is the whole of it. They are not returned and we do not want them returned. Twelve is about eighteen months of that station.

The department's own pages are here: [url=synth://ashkettlevfd.org/]ashkettlevfd.org[/url]. Their fundraising thermometer has read 62 percent since 2012 and the man who showed us where the tote goes made a joke about it before we could.

That brings the running total to 940 plus these twelve, which Marge will report properly in September because there is no August meeting.

posts.title: The August sew-in, and the outlets
posts.body:
Saturday 22 August, Nye Mills Grange hall, eight to four. Nineteen people. Moved off the 15th because that was fair weekend and half of us were in the exhibition hall.

$10 a head to the Grange for the hall, which is what they have charged since 2019 and which does not cover the propane in February. Bring your own machine, your own extension cord and a power strip.

[b]The outlets.[/b] There are four on the north wall and two on the south. The second one from the door on the north wall is on the same breaker as the kitchen, and the coffee urn is in the kitchen. If you are on it and somebody starts the urn, you are off. This has happened at every sew-in since at least 2017 and we have all agreed to fix it every time. The fix is a sign, and the sign would cost nothing, and there is no sign.

Twenty-six comfort tops finished, fourteen of them backed and basted. Two people worked only on their own block-of-the-month and were not made to feel bad about it.

Deb brought the Featherweight back running. It went to Sue Ann Ficke, who has been in the guild seven months and will use it, which was the condition. It sews a straight stitch and nothing else and it weighs eleven pounds and it will outlast every machine in that room.

Lunch was a potluck and there was too much of it, as there is every year, and the leftovers went home with the two people who brought the least, as they do every year.

Reva had the raffle quilt on the frame at the back and people sat down at it between things. Row 9. It comes off in early September.

posts.title: A quilt from a farm sale, and how old it is not
posts.body:
Carol Yaggi bought a quilt at a farm sale near Tessler for $30 and the man selling it told her it was from the 1860s. It came to the sew-in in a bin bag and eight people had their hands on it before nine in the morning. Here is what it is.

[b]It is a Grandmother's Flower Garden.[/b] Hexagons, English paper pieced over templates, three-quarter inch sides. The pattern is old but the craze for it in this country is 1925 to about 1940, and it is on the cover of every needlework page in the Ledger through the thirties.

[b]The backing is a feed sack.[/b] Printed, small rose, and you can see where two sacks were opened and seamed. Printed feed sacks run roughly 1925 to 1955 and that is the single most useful thing on the quilt.

[b]The fabrics are wrong for 1860.[/b] There are two double pinks and a cheddar in it that would pass, and people stop there. But there are also four solids in a mint, a peach, a lavender and a butter yellow that are 1930s dyes and are not 1860s anything, and there is a rayon blend in one flower that is later still, probably a repair.

[b]The batting is thin cotton with seeds in it.[/b] Everybody thinks the seeds mean early. They do not. Unginned cotton batting was sold into the 1950s and the seeds tell you it is cotton and cheap and nothing else.

[b]The quilting.[/b] Hand, outline quarter inch inside each hexagon, about seven stitches to the inch, one hand throughout. The binding is a separate straight-grain strip applied by machine on the front and finished by hand on the back, which is normal from the twenties on.

So: a 1930s quilt, almost certainly made from a kit or from a pattern in a paper, in good condition, with one later repair. Thirty dollars was fair and was probably low.

Nobody wants to hear that their quilt is ninety years old instead of a hundred and sixty. Ninety years old is a person's whole life. Somebody cut nine hundred hexagons out of the good parts of worn-out dresses and a feed sack, in a kitchen, at night, and then quilted it by hand, and it is still here, and it cost thirty dollars.

The library has the Ledger on microfilm from 1911 and the needlework column and the feed store advertisements are all in it. Karen will pull a reel for you: [url=synth://marchfieldlibrary.blog/]marchfieldlibrary.blog[/url]. The county fair's home arts department has been judging quilts since 1889 and the premium books are in the same collection: [url=synth://verity.wiki/wiki/county-fair]the fair[/url].

posts.title: The show is 3 October and here is what we need from you
posts.body:
Verity Piecers Quilt Show, Saturday 3 October, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., 4-H building at the fairgrounds. Admission $4, under 12 free. We do this every second year and the last one was 2024.

[b]Entries close Friday 25 September.[/b] Entry form to Bev Oakerson, $3 a quilt, three quilts maximum per member. Non-members may enter two at $5 each.

[b]Every quilt needs a sleeve and a label or it does not hang.[/b] This is not a preference, it is what the rods and the frames will take.

[list][*]Sleeve: 4 inches finished, so cut the strip 9 inches wide and hem the ends. Fold in half lengthwise, right sides out, seam it into a tube.[*]Ease: before you stitch it down, push about half an inch of slack into the tube along its length and pin that in. Without the ease the rod pulls a ridge across the front of the quilt and it shows in every photograph.[*]Stitch the sleeve down along the top and along the bottom, by hand, to the backing only. Not through to the front.[*]Ends 1 inch short of each side of the quilt.[*]Label sewn to the back, lower right corner: maker's name, the year, and who quilted it if it was not you.[/list]

[b]Classes[/b]

[list][*]1. Pieced, perimeter under 240 inches[*]2. Pieced, perimeter 240 inches and over[*]3. Applique[*]4. Mixed technique[*]5. Hand quilted by the maker[*]6. Machine quilted by the maker[*]7. Machine quilted by another, who must be named on the entry and on the label[*]8. Group quilt[*]9. First quilt, any technique, any age of maker[*]10. Small work, perimeter under 80 inches[/list]

Two judges. One is Loretta Kesterson from Bowes City, who judged in 2020 and was fair and slow. Ribbons in each class plus Best of Show and Viewer's Choice, which is a paper ballot and a coffee can.

[b]Handling.[/b] White gloves on the tables, one pair per person, and they are in a basket and they are not souvenirs. Do not turn a quilt over to look at the back unless a white-gloved member turns it for you. If a quilt has a card on it that says no photographs, that is the maker's decision and it is not up for discussion at the rail.

[b]The raffle quilt[/b] hangs alone on the north wall. Tickets at the door, $1 or six for $5. Drawn at 3:30 p.m.

[b]We still need[/b] two people Friday afternoon for hanging, four people on the door in two-hour shifts, and someone to run the kitchen who is not Marge, because Marge is doing the comfort quilt table and cannot be in two places.

posts.title: Minutes, September 10, 2026
posts.body:
Verity Piecers, regular meeting, Thursday 10 September 2026, community room, Marchfield Public Library. Called to order 6:30 p.m. exactly by Peg Sarnow, who noted it. Thirty-seven present, which is a record for a September and is the show.

Minutes of 9 July approved as posted. No meeting in August.

[b]Treasurer's report[/b] (Amsler), two months, there having been no August meeting. Balance 2 July, $2,880.40. In: dues $25, raffle tickets $442, show entry fees $87, sew-in hall money collected from nineteen people, $190. Out: hosting $18 for two months, Grange hall $190, balance on the ribbon order $52.30, photocopying the show book $41. Balance 3 September, $3,323.10.

Raffle to date: 1,586 tickets, $1,344, against 2,000 printed. Bev has four books still out and wants them in by the 25th, and the $64 from the picnic is still in an envelope in her kitchen.

[b]Comfort quilts[/b] (Feeney). Thirty-one out since July, which is the sew-in and the twelve to Ashkettle. Running total since 2009, [b]971[/b]. Marge said out loud that she would like to see a thousand before the end of next year and then said she should not have said it. The tops waiting on backs: fourteen.

[b]Raffle quilt[/b] (Oakerson). Off the frame Wednesday 2 September. Bound by Reva Detwiler, 2 and 1/4 inch double fold, mitred, joined on the bias, stitched down by hand on the back, which took her six evenings. Labelled. The label names Arla Wendt for the centre and the guild for the rest, which is what the June meeting decided.

[b]Fair report[/b] (Yaggi). Home arts. Class 12, pieced quilt over 72 inches: Nita Kohlman, first, $8. Class 13, pieced quilt under 72 inches: Bev Oakerson, second, $5. Class 16, hand quilting: one entry, Reva Detwiler, first, $8. Reva said afterwards that she entered it so the class would not be closed, because a class with no entries for two years comes out of the book, and once it is out of the book it does not go back in.

[b]Program.[/b] Carol Yaggi on binding, moved from June. Twenty-five minutes, mostly on joining the tail on the bias and why a 45 degree join on a straight-grain binding still matters.

[b]Show and tell.[/b] Nine blocks. Sue Ann Ficke brought four, all done in the last three weeks on an eleven-pound machine from 1952, and said the plan had held.

[b]Old business.[/b] Show, 3 October. Hanging crew has twelve names and we needed ten. Door shifts full. Kitchen is Gail Prine.

[b]New business.[/b] Website. Ellen reported the domain renews 14 November at $18 and hosting is $9 a month and the guild has been paying it out of Dot's card and reimbursing since 2011. Motion by Hesch that the guild open a card in the guild's name so this stops being one person's problem, second by Sarnow, carried 35-0. Dot said it had never been a problem and that she would take the card anyway.

Adjourned 8:37 p.m. Next meeting 8 October, which is five days after the show, so bring your feet up.

Respectfully submitted, E. Vraber, secretary.
